name: Representation
definition: International IDEA's Representation attribute measures whether people have free and equal access to political power through credible elections, inclusive suffrage, free political parties, elected government, effective parliament, and local democracy.
interpretation: Higher scores indicate stronger representative institutions relative to the full country-year sample; the score is one dimension of democracy, not an overall democracy ranking.
whyItMatters: Representation connects public preferences to decision makers and shows whether electoral choice is translated into accountable political authority.
caveat: This is a modelled composite with uncertainty intervals. Small score differences may not be meaningful, and International IDEA advises against collapsing its dimensions into one democracy score.

name: Credible elections
definition: The extent to which elections are free from irregularities, intimidation, government manipulation, and systematic barriers to genuine competition.
interpretation: Higher scores indicate electoral processes that more reliably allow voters to choose among genuine alternatives.
whyItMatters: Elections cannot provide democratic accountability when administration, competition, campaigning, or vote counting is not credible.
caveat: The estimate combines several coded and expert-assessed inputs and carries uncertainty; it does not by itself measure all aspects of democracy between elections.

name: Effective parliament
definition: The extent to which the legislature is capable of overseeing the executive and exercising meaningful influence over public policy.
interpretation: Higher scores suggest stronger legislative checks and a more consequential role for parliament beyond formally approving executive decisions.
whyItMatters: Effective legislatures scrutinize government, represent competing interests, and reduce unchecked concentration of executive power.
caveat: Formal constitutional powers and practical influence can differ; this composite depends partly on expert assessments and should be read with its uncertainty.

name: Rights
definition: International IDEA's Rights attribute combines access to justice, civil liberties, basic welfare, and political equality as foundations for meaningful democratic participation.
interpretation: Higher scores indicate broader realization of liberal and social rights that enable people to participate as political equals.
whyItMatters: Political choice is not substantively equal when people lack basic liberties, legal redress, security, or the resources needed to participate.
caveat: This broad composite combines distinct concepts. Inspect its subcomponents rather than treating similar overall scores as evidence of identical rights conditions.

name: Civil liberties
definition: The extent to which freedom of expression, press, association and assembly, religion, and movement are respected.
interpretation: Higher values indicate that people can more freely communicate, organize, worship, assemble, and move.
whyItMatters: Civil liberties allow opposition, journalism, civic organization, and ordinary people to challenge power and participate in public life.
caveat: National scores can hide differences among groups and regions; the estimate aggregates several sources and includes model uncertainty.

name: Freedom of the press
definition: The extent to which media can report and comment on political issues without censorship, harassment, or undue political control.
interpretation: Higher scores indicate a media environment with greater editorial freedom and less coercive restriction.
whyItMatters: Independent journalism helps people evaluate government performance, exposes wrongdoing, and broadens the information available for public debate.
caveat: The score does not directly measure media concentration, business-model fragility, misinformation, or every form of online information control.

name: Gender equality in democratic participation
definition: A GSoD subcomponent measuring the extent to which women and men have equal political power and access to relevant social and economic resources.
interpretation: Higher scores indicate a narrower gender gap in the conditions and power needed for equal democratic participation.
whyItMatters: A political system cannot provide equal popular control when gender strongly determines voice, representation, or access to power.
caveat: This is not the same as UNDP's Gender Inequality Index: the concepts, components, scale, and direction differ, and neither captures every gender identity or intersectional disparity.

name: Rule of law
definition: International IDEA's Rule of Law attribute combines judicial independence, absence of corruption, predictable enforcement, and personal integrity and security.
interpretation: Higher scores indicate that public authority is more constrained, impartial, predictable, and protective of personal security.
whyItMatters: Democratic rights and decisions depend on rules being enforced consistently rather than arbitrarily or selectively.
caveat: This is a modelled composite and differs conceptually from the World Bank governance percentile; use the subcomponents to understand why a score is high or low.

name: Judicial independence
definition: The extent to which courts are independent of political influence and can constrain government according to law.
interpretation: Higher values indicate greater practical autonomy of the judiciary from the executive and other political actors.
whyItMatters: Independent courts are central to legal redress, rights protection, enforcement of constitutional limits, and peaceful resolution of disputes.
caveat: Formal guarantees do not always equal practical independence, and expert-based inputs introduce uncertainty that matters for close comparisons.

name: Absence of corruption
definition: The extent to which the executive, legislature, judiciary, and public administration exercise authority without using public office for private gain.
interpretation: Higher values indicate fewer signs of corruption across key branches and levels of public authority.
whyItMatters: Corruption can redirect public resources, weaken equal treatment, distort representation, and reduce trust in collective institutions.
caveat: Hidden conduct is difficult to observe. This composite is partly perception- and expert-based and should not be read as a count of proven corruption cases.

name: Participation
definition: International IDEA's Participation attribute combines civil society, civic engagement, electoral participation, and opportunities for direct democracy.
interpretation: Higher scores indicate that people make greater use of, and have stronger opportunities for, participation beyond simply having formal political rights.
whyItMatters: Democratic institutions are more responsive when people can organize and participate in elections, civic life, and public decision-making.
caveat: High participation is not automatically inclusive or rights-respecting, and the component measures should be inspected separately.

name: Civil society
definition: The extent to which organized, voluntary civic groups can form, operate, participate, and scrutinize public authority independently of the state.
interpretation: Higher scores indicate a more autonomous, active, and enabling environment for civic organization.
whyItMatters: Civil society connects people, surfaces neglected interests, provides services and knowledge, and creates channels for accountability between elections.
caveat: A national score cannot show which groups are excluded, how organizations are financed, or whether civic space differs across regions and issues.

name: Political regime type
unit: four-category Regimes of the World classification
definition: The Regimes of the World classification groups political systems as closed autocracies, electoral autocracies, electoral democracies, or liberal democracies using V-Dem data processed by Our World in Data.
interpretation: The value is an ordered category, not a continuous score: it describes a broad regime family and should be read alongside the more specific democracy dimensions.
whyItMatters: A categorical classification gives a legible starting point for the overall institutional regime while the component indicators show where democratic strengths and weaknesses lie.
caveat: Borderline cases are uncertain, categories simplify complex systems, and equal numerical steps must not be interpreted as equal substantive distances.

name: General government debt
definition: The total stock of debt liabilities issued by general government, expressed as a share of gross domestic product, from the IMF Global Debt Database.
interpretation: The ratio compares the scale of government debt with annual economic output; it is not a direct measure of whether debt is affordable or sustainable.
whyItMatters: Debt can finance investment and stabilize shocks, but its level, interest cost, currency, maturity, and creditor structure shape fiscal room and vulnerability.
caveat: Coverage and institutional boundaries differ across countries. Compare alongside interest costs, revenue, growth, currency composition, assets, and whether the figure is gross or net.

name: Private debt, loans and debt securities
definition: Loans and debt securities issued by households and nonfinancial corporations, expressed as a share of GDP, from the IMF Global Debt Database.
interpretation: The ratio shows the size of private-sector borrowing relative to the economy, not whether borrowing is productive or financially fragile.
whyItMatters: Private leverage can support homes and investment but can also amplify financial crises, depress demand after shocks, and transfer risk to the public sector.
caveat: This measure excludes some debt instruments and financial-sector debt. Cross-country financial structures and data coverage differ, so use it with household and corporate breakdowns.

name: Household debt, loans and debt securities
definition: Loans and debt securities owed by households, expressed as a share of GDP, from the IMF Global Debt Database.
interpretation: Higher ratios indicate more household borrowing relative to economic output but do not show which households owe the debt or what assets secure it.
whyItMatters: Household leverage affects housing markets, consumption, inequality, financial stability, and sensitivity to interest-rate or income shocks.
caveat: Coverage is substantially narrower than for total private debt, and ratios should be interpreted with income, wealth, interest costs, mortgage structure, and borrower distribution.

name: Nonfinancial corporate debt, loans and debt securities
definition: Loans and debt securities issued by nonfinancial corporations, expressed as a share of GDP, from the IMF Global Debt Database.
interpretation: Higher ratios indicate greater corporate borrowing relative to the economy, but not whether firms can service it or whether it financed productive assets.
whyItMatters: Corporate leverage can accelerate investment and growth while increasing refinancing, insolvency, banking, and employment risks during downturns.
caveat: Coverage is narrower than for total private debt and may not capture all instruments or offshore structures; sector mix and state-owned enterprises also affect comparability.

name: Military expenditure
definition: Military expenditure as a share of GDP, based on the SIPRI Military Expenditure Database distributed through World Development Indicators.
interpretation: The ratio shows the share of annual economic output devoted to military purposes, not the absolute size, effectiveness, or necessity of spending.
whyItMatters: Defense commitments compete with other uses of resources and can reveal security priorities, conflict pressures, and the fiscal weight of the military sector.
caveat: Definitions, secrecy, off-budget activity, and treatment of military pensions or paramilitary forces vary. International comparisons are estimates, not precise audits.

name: Military expenditure share of government spending
definition: Military expenditure as a percentage of general government expenditure, based on SIPRI estimates where comparable government-spending data permit.
interpretation: The ratio shows how much of reported government expenditure is allocated to the military and can be compared with health and education shares.
whyItMatters: Budget shares make public priorities visible even when countries differ greatly in economic size and overall government spending.
caveat: The denominator and institutional coverage can vary; secrecy and off-budget military activity can understate spending, and the latest year may differ from other budget-share indicators.

name: Government education expenditure share
definition: Current, capital, and transfer spending on education by general government as a percentage of total government expenditure, reported by UNESCO UIS through World Development Indicators.
interpretation: The ratio shows education's share of the government budget; a larger share is not automatically sufficient, equitable, or effective.
whyItMatters: Education budgets shape access, staffing, infrastructure, learning conditions, and long-term capabilities while revealing one major public priority.
caveat: Government coverage, fiscal years, and reporting quality differ. Compare with spending per learner, outcomes, demographics, private costs, and the size of the total public budget.

name: Government health expenditure share
definition: Domestic general government health expenditure as a percentage of total general government expenditure, from WHO health accounts distributed through World Development Indicators.
interpretation: The ratio shows the priority given to health within public spending, not the total resources available or the quality and equity of care.
whyItMatters: Public financing strongly affects access to essential care, financial protection, system capacity, and the distribution of health risks.
caveat: It excludes private and external spending and can be affected by accounting boundaries. Read it with expenditure per person, service coverage, outcomes, and out-of-pocket costs.
